en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpāna-vagga 52.
The Training Rule on Prodding with the Fingers.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks made the monk from the group of seventeen laugh by tickling him with their fingers.
That monk died, gasping and unable to breathe.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the group of six monks amuse a monk by tickling him with their fingers?
… [after investigating] … “Is it true, monks, that you amuse a monk by tickling him with your fingers?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, make a monk laugh by tickling him with your fingers?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"In tickling with the fingers, there is an offense of expiation.
Now, what is called "tickling with the fingers"?
If one who is ordained, with the intention of causing laughter, touches the body of another who is ordained with his own body, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one perceives another as ordained when they are indeed ordained, and makes them laugh by poking them with a finger, there is an offense of expiation.
If one is uncertain whether another is ordained when they are indeed ordained, and makes them laugh by poking them with a finger, there is an offense of expiation.
If one makes a person who is fully ordained laugh by tickling them with a finger while perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches the body with something connected to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is attached to the body with what is attached to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches the body with what has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches what is attached to the body with what has been relinquished, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches an article that ought to be relinquished with an article that ought to be relinquished, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one touches with the body the body of one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If one touches with the body something connected to the body [of one who is not fully ordained], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with something connected to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she touches something connected to another’s body with something connected to her own body, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she touches her body with something that has been relinquished (nissaggiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one touches something attached to the body with something that has been forfeited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one touches something that has been forfeited with something that has been forfeited, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is doubtful that the person is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
There is no offense if it was not with the intention of laughing,
if he touches her while there is a purpose to be served,
or if he is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
the second training rule concerning the poking with the finger is finished.
